# Examples from `coord_radial()` documentation {#sec-coord-radial} 

Version 3.5.0 of `ggplot2` introducted `coord_radial()`, a modernized polar coordinate system adds three key capabilities over `coord_polar()`:

- **Partial arcs** via an `end` argument (any arc from a sliver to a full circle).
- **Inner radius** (`inner_radius`) to create donut and gauge charts.
- **Radial-axis placement** (`r_axis_inside`) and optional angle-aesthetic
  rotation (`rotate_angle`).

The examples below are adapted from the
[ggplot2 reference page](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_radial.html).

::: {.callout-caution}
All of the examples on this page require the `coord-polar` branch of
[iangow/plotnine](https://github.com/iangow/plotnine/tree/coord-polar).
The standard version of plotnine does not include the `coord_polar()` and `coord_radial()` functions used here.
:::

```{python}
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import plotnine_polars as p9
from plotnine.data import mtcars
from plotnine_polars import aes
```

::: {.callout-note}
In this chapter, I use `plotnine_polars`, a package with that does two things with less than 100 lines of code.
First, it reexports all the functions from `plotnine` as methods that can be used with plot objects created by `plotnine`.
Second, it creates a custom `ggplot` namespace for Polars `DataFrame` objects so that plots can be created using a `.ggplot.plot()` method or using the simple `.ggplot()` shortcut.^[Basically, the `__call__` method of the `ggplot` namespace is mapped to `.plot()`.]

In this way, `plotnine_polars` allows me to use method chains to access most of the functionality of `plotnine` without having to do things like running `from plotnine import *` or creating intermediate variables.^[To be fair, the `>>` operator in `plotnine` already addresses the second item.]
Instead, the only thing I explicitly import from `plotnine` is `aes()`.
:::



```{python}
mtcars_pl = (
    pl.from_pandas(mtcars)
    .with_columns(
        pl.lit("1").alias("x"),
        pl.col("cyl").cast(pl.Utf8),
    )
)
```

## Pie chart

A stacked bar chart becomes a pie chart under `coord_radial(theta="y")`.
This is the `coord_radial()` equivalent of the `coord_polar()` pie chart.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-pie
#| fig-cap: "Pie chart with `coord_radial(theta='y')`"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(theta="y", expand=False)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Coxcomb chart

A **coxcomb chart** or **rose chart** maps each discrete category to an equal angular slice but lets the bar *height* encode the count [@sec-night provides a deeper example of a coxcomb chart.]
This is the default `theta="x"` orientation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-coxcomb
#| fig-cap: "Coxcomb chart: bar heights encode count, angles encode category"
cxc = (
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1, color="black")
)

(   cxc
    .coord_radial(expand=False)
    .add_theme(figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-coxcomb2
#| fig-cap: "Coxcomb chart: bar heights encode count, angles encode category"
(   cxc
    .coord_radial(theta="y", expand=False)
    .add_theme(figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Bullseye chart

Swapping the aesthetics — stacking the cyl groups on a single x position with
`theta="x"` — produces concentric rings (a bullseye).

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-bullseye
#| fig-cap: "Bullseye chart: coord_radial() with a stacked single-bar"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(expand=False)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```


```{python}
df = pl.DataFrame({
  "variable": ["does not resemble", "resembles"],
  "value":[20, 80]
})
```

```{python}
import math

(
    df
    .ggplot(aes(x=1, y="value", fill="variable"))
    .geom_col(width = 1)
    .scale_fill_manual(values=["red", "yellow"])
    .coord_radial("y", start = math.pi / 3, expand=False)
    .labs(title = "Pac-Man")
)
```

## Donut chart

Setting `inner_radius` pushes data away from the centre, leaving a hollow
hole.  The value is a fraction of the outer radius, so `inner_radius=0.3`
creates a 30 % hole.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-donut
#| fig-cap: "Donut chart: inner_radius=0.3 carves a hole in the pie"
(
    mtcars_pl
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", fill="cyl"))
    .geom_bar(width=1)
    .coord_radial(theta="y", expand=False, inner_radius=0.3)
    .scale_x_discrete(expand=(0, 0))
    .scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```

## Pac-Man chart

Combining `theta="y"` with a non-zero `start` angle cuts a wedge out of the
pie.  A start of `π/3` (60°) creates Hadley Wickham's favourite illustration
of why pie charts are hard to read.

```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-pacman
#| fig-cap: "Pac-Man: coord_radial(theta='y', start=π/3)"
pac_data = pl.DataFrame({
    "variable": ["does not resemble", "resembles"],
    "value": [20, 80],
    "x": ["", ""],
})

(
    pac_data
    .ggplot(aes(x="x", y="value", fill="variable"))
    .geom_col(width=1)
    .scale_fill_manual(values={"does not resemble": "red", "resembles": "yellow"})
    .coord_radial(theta="y", start=np.pi / 3, expand=False)
    .labs(title="Pac Man")
    .add_theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(4, 4))
)
```



## Partial polar scatter

Providing both `start` and `end` limits the plot to an arc rather than a
full circle.  Combined with `inner_radius`, this is the basis for gauge and
fan charts.  Here `mtcars` displacement is mapped to angle and fuel economy
to radius.


```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-partial
#| fig-cap: "Partial polar scatter: start/end define the arc, inner_radius adds a hole"
(
    pl.from_pandas(mtcars)
    .ggplot(aes(x="disp", y="mpg"))
    .geom_point()
    .coord_radial(start=-0.4 * np.pi, end=0.4 * np.pi, inner_radius=0.3)
    .add_theme(figure_size=(5, 5))
)
```

`thetalim` and `rlim` zoom into a data-space window on each axis without removing
points — equivalent to `coord_cartesian(xlim=..., ylim=...)` in Cartesian space.

::: {.callout-note}
The original ggplot2 [plot](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/coord_radial-8.png) for the following looks wrong, as there are points in the middle of nowhere.
:::


```{python}
#| label: fig-radial-partial-zoom
#| fig-cap: "Partial polar scatter with thetalim and rlim zooming into a data window"
(
    pl.from_pandas(mtcars)
    .ggplot(aes(x="disp", y="mpg"))
    .geom_point()
    .coord_radial(
        start=-0.4 * np.pi, end=0.4 * np.pi,
        inner_radius=0.3,
        thetalim=(200, 300),
        rlim=(15, 30),
    )
    .add_theme(figure_size=(5, 5))
)
```
